text:
SWIFT ENERGY NEW ZEALAND LIMITED

The Ahuroa South B-1 well was designed as a directional appraisal well to test the hydrocarbon potential of the McKee Sand reservoir in a position approximately 825 m southeast of the Ahuroa pad. The well was planned to test a downdip location structurally equivalent to that drilled in the Piakau North A-2 location. The well was drilled from the existing Ahuroa B well site.

In the proposal the McKee Sand was to be intersected at 3180 m MD and the well was proposed to reach a TD of 3430 m. The McKee Sands were actually encountered at 3230 m MD, 59 m deep TVDSS to prognosis. This put the McKee Sands penetrated in this location below the estimated water contact for the field. A TD was called at 3370 m MD and wireline logs were run confirming that the McKee Sands were not hydrocarbon bearing in this location. The well was sidetracked from 2400 m MD to try and intersect the McKee Sands at an updip location; however, in Ahuroa South B-1 ST1, the McKee Sands were not developed.

The well was spudded on 5 October 2005 and the rig released on 28 November 2005.

text:
The Ahuroa South B-1 well was designed as a directional appraisal well to test the hydrocarbon potential of the McKee Sand reservoir in a position approximately 825 m south-east of the Ahuroa pad. The well was designed to test a down dip location structurally equivalent to that drilled in the Piakau North A-2 location (2800 m TVDSS). This well was to test the theory of a deeper OWC (2825 m TVDSS).

The McKee Sand was to be intersected at 3180 m MD and the well was proposed to reach a TD of 3430 m.

The well was spudded on 5 October 2005 and a 12 ¼" hole was drilled from 50 to 659 m. 13 3/8" casing was set with the casing shoe at 653. The 8 ½" hole was drilled to 2403 m. Wireline logs were run and then 7" casing was run and cemented with the casing shoe set at 2395 m.

A 6" hole was drilled through the Tariki Sand and down through the McKee Sand. At 3340 m, the well drilled through the main thrust into the younger Manganui Formation. The well was drilled to a TD of 3370 m MD and then logged. A side-track, Ahuroa South B-1 ST1 was drilled with a 6" hole from the kick-off point (2400 m) to a final TD of 3085 m MD. After wireline logs were run, the well was plugged and abandoned.

The rig was released on 28 November 2005.

(Note: All depths are quoted as MD, measured by wireline logs below the rotary table ("RT"), sometimes kelly bushing ("KB"), unless otherwise specified. TVDSS denotes true vertical depth below mean sea level in metres)

The well was spudded on 5 October 2005. The McKee Sands were encountered at 3230 m MD (2884.1 m TVDSS), 59 m TVDSS deep to prognosis (2825 m TVDSS), and below the oil-water contact. The well failed to meet the primary objective of penetrating a hydrocarbon bearing McKee Sand section. The well was drilled to a total depth of 3370 m MD and wireline logs were run. These logs confirming that the McKee Sands were not hydrocarbon bearing at this location.

The well was side-tracked from 2400 m MD to intersect the McKee Sands at an up-dip location, but on Ahuroa South B-1 ST1 the McKee Sands were not developed. The final TD was at 3085 m MD after drilling into the Mangahewa from 2981 m MD. The well was plugged and abandoned and the rig moved to the Kauri F-2 site.

The structurally diverse Taranaki Basin lies along the west coast of New Zealand's North Island, south of Auckland and northwest of Wellington, and also along the northwest coast of the South Island, northwest of Nelson. Located at the convergent boundary between the Australian Plate (west New Zealand) and the Pacific Plate (east New Zealand), the Taranaki Basin is a product of several phases of basin evolution. It covers approximately 100,000 square kilometers (38,610 square miles), of which about 90% is offshore.

The Taranaki Basin is elongated in a north-south direction and is principally a subsurface feature, the onshore portion of which lies beneath a surficial cover of Quaternary volcanic and alluvial deposits. Sediments in the basin are up to nine kilometers thick and range in age from Cretaceous to Recent. The buried Taranaki Fault bounds the basin on the east, while the western boundary of the basin is effectively the deep-water platform Challenger Plateau.

The northern and southern limits of the basin are not as well defined. In the south, the Taranaki Basin is today topographically emergent and is evident on the northwest coast of the South Island in the form of Cretaceous cored ridges and sub-basins. To the north, the Taranaki Basin merges with the predominantly offshore Northland Basin and the abyssal New Caledonia Basin.

The Taranaki Basin can be readily divided between the Eastern Mobile Belt (Taranaki Graben) and the Western Stable Platform. All proved hydrocarbon accumulations lie either within or at the flank of the Eastern Mobile Belt. Maui Field, the largest in New Zealand, is at the boundary between these two provinces.

The Eastern Mobile Belt can be divided into a number of sub-provinces: Northern Graben, Central Graben, Tarata/Taranaki Fault Trend, and the Southern Inversion Zone.

The Northern Graben, which is entirely offshore north and northwest of the Taranaki Peninsula, is an area of late Miocene to Pliocene extension bounded on the west by the Cape Egmont Fault Zone and on the east by the Turi Fault Zone. The Cape Egmont Fault Zone marks the western limit of deformation of the overriding Australian Plate.

The Central Graben area, manifested both onshore and offshore, lies to the south of the Northern Graben area, but is slightly younger and represents the southward migration of the extension related to the complex interrelationships of the Australian and Pacific Plate boundaries. As with the Northern Graben region, the Central Graben region is bounded on the west by the Cape Egmont Fault Zone and on the east by a system of normal faults that trend northeast-southwest.

metadata.section_path: 4.0 GEOLOGY, GEOPHYSICS, FORMATION SAMPLING AND EVALUATION

text:
The Tarata/Taranaki Fault Trend lies immediately to the west of the Patea-Tongaporutu High basement block complex, along the eastern margin of the basin. The Taranaki Fault Zone is a major reverse fault that offsets the basement by more than 5 kilometers (3.1 miles). This westward directed fault was active throughout much of the Miocene. Sediments of late Miocene and younger cover the upthrust Patea-Tongaporutu High basement block east of the Taranaki Fault. This sediment cover continues eastward into the North and South Wanganui Basins. The Tarata Fault Zone, a region of generally thin-skinned thrust faults, is immediately west of, and associated with, the Taranaki Fault Zone. The Tarata Fault Zone is comprised of generally west directed faults that were active during the early Miocene. McKee, Waihapa, Tariki, and Ngaere are examples of Tarata Fault trend fields. The Southern Inversion Zone covers the southern reaches of the basin. This is an area of large-scale structural inversion of former rift half-grabens. The Southern Inversion Zone contains a number of reverse fault bounded inverted anticlines. The large Kapuni Field and the Kupe South Field along the Manaia anticline are examples of productive structures within this region. The latter two sub-provinces cover PML 38139 and contain the majority of the fields found to date.

The Western Stable Platform is largely unexplored and results to date have been discouraging. This area has been relatively tectonically inactive since the Paleocene, showing little evidence of deformation except for flexure to the east caused by sediment loading.

The Taranaki Basin is filled with sediment ranging in age from late Cretaceous to Recent. The entire sedimentary sequence may be summarized as an overall major transgressive cycle beginning in the late Cretaceous and continuing to the early Miocene. This was followed by an overall regressive phase, which continues today. The majority of reservoirs within the basin are clastic, aside from the fractured Tikorangi Limestone, which produces at Waihapa/Ngaere.

Oil has been produced in the Taranaki Basin since 1865 at the shallow Moturoa Field near New Plymouth. In this field, the oil reservoir is in the Miocene-Pliocene shelf sands of the Matemateaonga Formation. This remained the only producing area in the Taranaki Basin until the discovery in 1959 of the onshore Kapuni Field which produces gas-condensate from the Eocene level sands. Hydrocarbon reserves have been found within all major chronostratigraphic levels except the Cretaceous. The lack of Cretaceous age reservoirs may simply be a function of a lack of wells penetrating to this level.

The oldest proven reservoir in the Taranaki is the Paleocene Farewell Formation. This unit produces at the Kupe South Field and the Maui Field. The major reservoirs in the basin occur in the Eocene to early Miocene interval. The older reservoirs (Eocene and older) in the western portion of the basin (e.g., in the Maui Field and the Kapuni Field) tend to be gas-condensate, whereas those along the eastern flank of the basin in younger age rocks, latest Eocene and younger (e.g., in the McKee Field and Waihapa Field), are often oil bearing. The estimated known total remaining reserves in the Taranaki Basin are 54.5 MMBO and 1320.6 BCF with 0.8 MM tonnes LPG (Crown Minerals Data, 2002).

The major source for the hydrocarbons produced in the Taranaki Basin are the coals and carbonaceous shales deposited in the coastal plains and swamps of the Late Cretaceous Pakawau group and Paleocene-Eocene Kapuni groups. It is estimated that only about 1% of the hydrocarbons generated by the Rakopi Formation (Pakawau group) in the eastern region of the Taranaki Basin have been discovered to date.

text:
The Ahuroa South B-1 well was designed as a directional appraisal well to test the hydrocarbon potential of the McKee Sand reservoir in a position approximately 825 m south-east of the Ahuroa pad. The well was designed to test a down dip location structurally equivalent to that drilled in the Piakau North A-2 location.

The well was to be drilled from the existing Ahuroa B well-site. The McKee Sand was to be intersected at 3180 m MD. The well was proposed to reach a TD of 3430 m.

Tariki sands were water-wet in both Ahuroa South B-1 and ST1, as expected. McKee sands were encountered 59 m deep to prognosis in Ahuroa South B-1, well below the oil-water contact, and were water-wet. McKee sands were not developed in Ahuroa South B-1 ST1.

A revised geological picture would therefore suggest that the McKee Sand both thins to the north and to the west in the Ahuroa South area. The sand likely thickens in the direction of the Manutahi Pub.

The stratigraphy in Ahuroa South B-1 and ST1 was similar to that seen in other wells in Ahuroa Field.

The following is a generalized description on formations drilled along with any fluorescence descriptions for Ahuroa South B-1 / ST1.

The Urenui Formation is predominantly claystone with siltstone, sandstone and limestone beds.

CLAYSTONE: The claystone is greenish grey to dark greenish grey, light bluish grey, medium grey and olive grey. The cuttings are predominantly very soft to soft, although they range from very soft to firm. They are largely amorphous to blocky. The claystone is generally non calcareous but is slightly to very calcareous in parts. Accessories include a trace to minor presence of shell fragments in parts, trace to common very fine lower to fine upper quartz sand grains in parts and minor to common glauconite pellets. This claystone has an arenaceous nature in parts.

SILTSTONE: The siltstone is olive grey in colour. The cuttings are soft and were amorphous to sub-blocky. The siltstone is non calcareous and grades to sandstone.

SANDSTONE: The sandstone is mainly unconsolidated, transparent to translucent, quartz grains, with aggregates that are predominantly coloured light olive grey to greenish grey and medium bluish grey in parts. The aggregates are mostly firm to hard, although they range from soft to hard. The grain size ranges from very fine lower to medium lower, predominantly very fine upper to fine upper. They are sub-angular to sub-rounded in shape and are moderately to well sorted. The sandstone has an argillaceous cement in some parts and calcite cement in others, and is moderately to very calcareous in parts. Accessories include minor to common levels of glauconite, traces of shell fragments, and traces of mica. The sandstone has poor inferred porosity.

LIMESTONE: The limestone is predominantly white to light grey. The aggregates are firm to hard and are sub-blocky in shape. The limestone is arenaceous and the grains are very fine upper to fine lower in size. There is a minor component of shell fragments. The limestone grades to sandstone.

The Mt Messenger Formation is predominantly claystone inter-bedded with sandstone, siltstone and limestone.

CLAYSTONE: The claystone is predominantly light olive grey to olive grey, though it is greenish grey to dark greenish grey, medium bluish grey, and medium dark grey in parts. The cuttings are very soft to firm and sub-blocky to blocky in form. There is an arenaceous component to the claystone, with traces of quartz sand grains ranging in size from very fine lower to very fine upper. The claystone is slightly to very calcareous in parts and grades to siltstone.

SILTSTONE: The colour of the siltstone in this formation is greenish grey to dark greenish grey, and light olive grey to olive black. The cuttings are firm to hard and are sub-blocky to blocky in form. The claystone is moderately to very calcareous, and grades to claystone.

SANDSTONE: The sandstone is predominantly unconsolidated, transparent to translucent quartz, with light to dark grey aggregates. The aggregates are firm to hard and the grains range in size from very fine lower to coarse lower, though are predominantly fine upper to medium upper. The grains are sub-angular to sub-rounded in shape and range from poorly to well sorted. The aggregates are calcite cemented. The sandstone has no visible porosity; however, have moderate inferred porosity in parts determined by the size, shape and rounding of the unconsolidated grains.

LIMESTONE: The colour of the limestone is light olive grey. The cuttings are firm to hard and are sub-blocky in shape. There is an arenaceous component to the limestone. The limestone grades to claystone.

The Tikorangi Formation is primarily limestone with siltstone interbeds.

LIMESTONE: The limestone has a range in colour from white to light grey and olive grey. The limestone is arenaceous in nature. The cuttings are generally very soft to firm, but are hard in parts and are sub-blocky to blocky in form. Traces of pyrite are present at the top of the formation. The limestone grades to siltstone, and also grades to claystone at the top of the section.

SILTSTONE: The siltstone ranges in colour from medium grey, medium bluish grey, olive grey, and greenish grey to dark greenish grey. The cuttings are soft to hard and are sub-blocky to blocky in form. The siltstone is moderately to very calcareous. There are minor amounts of carbonaceous material in parts. It grades to claystone and limestone in parts.

The Upper Otaraoa Formation consists of siltstone at the top of the section becoming mainly claystone towards the base of the section, with limestone inter-beds.

CLAYSTONE: The claystone is light olive grey to olive black, dark greenish grey and medium grey. The cuttings range from soft to hard, though predominantly soft to firm. They are sub-blocky to blocky in shape. There is a trace to common component of calcite veins, and the claystone is slightly to very calcareous, though predominantly moderately calcareous. The claystone grades to siltstone in parts.

SILTSTONE: The colour of the siltstone is predominantly light olive grey to olive grey, although it is greenish grey to dark greenish grey and bluish grey in parts. The cuttings are soft to firm though they are hard in parts. They are sub-blocky to blocky in form. The siltstone is argillaceous in parts, and also has a minor component of carbonaceous material in parts. The siltstone is moderately to very calcareous throughout the section, however it gradually becomes less calcareous towards the base of the section. The siltstone grades to claystone and limestone in parts.

LIMESTONE: The limestone is olive grey to medium grey in colour. The cuttings are very soft to hard and are sub-blocky to blocky in form. The limestone is arenaceous and grades to siltstone.

text:
2714 – 3145 m MD

The Tariki Sandstone is sandstone with siltstone, claystone and limestone beds.

SANDSTONE: The sandstone is predominantly transparent to translucent quartz, with some white to dark grey, and yellowish grey aggregates. It is mostly unconsolidated, with a minor amount of soft to very hard aggregates. The grains range in size from very fine lower to coarse upper, and are sub-angular to rounded. The grains are predominantly moderately to well sorted, although there are some poorly sorted examples. The cement is calcareous and there are trace amounts of glauconite, coal and carbonaceous material present in parts. Rock flour is also common in the cuttings. There is poor to good inferred porosity.

SILTSTONE: The siltstone is olive grey to olive black, and light to dark grey in parts. The cuttings are firm and are sub-blocky to blocky in shape. The siltstone has a slightly to moderately calcareous character and grades to claystone in parts.

CLAYSTONE: The claystone is light olive grey to olive grey, and is dark grey in parts. Cuttings range from very soft to hard although are mainly soft to firm. The cuttings are predominantly sub-blocky to blocky in form, although amorphous in parts. The claystone ranges from non calcareous to moderately calcareous and grades to siltstone in parts.

LIMESTONE: The limestone is white to light grey. Cuttings range from soft to firm and are sub-blocky to blocky. The limestone is arenaceous in parts and has minor to common amounts of very fine upper to medium upper quartz grains. The limestone grades to very calcareous sandstone.

3145 – 3230 m MD

The Lower Otaraoa Formation consists of interbedded claystone and siltstone with minor amounts of sandstone.

CLAYSTONE: The claystone is light olive grey to olive grey in colour. The cuttings are soft to firm, with occasional very hard cuttings in parts. Their form is sub-blocky to blocky. The claystone is slightly to moderately calcareous, and grades to limestone at the top of the section. It also grades to siltstone in parts.

SILTSTONE: The siltstone is coloured dark greenish grey to greenish black. The cuttings range from soft to firm and are sub-blocky to blocky in form. Glauconite is common in the siltstone. The siltstone is very calcareous, and grades to claystone.

SANDSTONE: The sandstone is loose transparent to translucent quartz. The grains range in size from very fine lower to fine upper, are sub-rounded and moderately sorted. There is fair inferred porosity in the sandstone.

3230 – 3244.8 m MD

The McKee Formation consists of interbedded sandstone and siltstone.

SANDSTONE: The sandstone is light grey to yellow grey aggregates. The cuttings are friable. The grains range in size from very fine lower to fine lower. The grains are sub-angular to sub-rounded in shape and moderately well sorted. There is abundant silty matrix present and traces of loose transparent to translucent quartz. There is poor visible porosity observed.

SILTSTONE: The siltstone is mostly white to yellowish grey, but is also dark greenish grey to greenish black. The cuttings are sub-blocky to blocky in shape and are soft to firm. Glauconite is common with the lighter siltstone. The darker siltstone is very calcareous, and the lighter is slightly calcareous in parts. The siltstone grades to sandstone.

The Mangahewa Formation is comprised primarily of claystone, interbedded with minor layers of siltstone, sandstone and coal seams. The lower contact of this formation is marked by the Ahuroa Thrust system.

SILTSTONE: The siltstone is coloured dark greenish grey to greenish black. The cuttings range from soft to firm and are sub-blocky to blocky in form. Glauconite is common in the siltstone. The siltstone is very calcareous, and grades to claystone.

SANDSTONE: The sandstone is loose transparent to translucent quartz. The grains range in size from very fine lower to fine upper, are sub-rounded and moderately sorted. There is fair inferred porosity in the sandstone.

MCKEE FORMATION: 2972 – 2985 m MD AHUROA SOUTH B-1 ST1

The McKee Formation is represented by a thin sequence of claystone and siltstone with minor sandstone. The McKee Sands are not developed.

CLAYSTONE: Olive grey, light olive grey, soft – firm, amorphous – subblocky, moderately calcareous.

SILTSTONE: Dark greenish grey – greyish black, soft – firm, blocky, moderately calcareous, abundant glauconite. Light grey, yellowish grey, soft – firm, blocky, moderately calcareous, trace very fine quartz grains, trace glauconite

SANDSTONE: Yellowish grey, friable, very fine lower – medium upper, predominantly fine lower, moderately sorted, subangular – rounded, trace calcareous cement, trace glauconite, abundant silty matrix, grades to siltstone, poor – fair porosity, no show

MANGAHEWA FORMATION: 2985 – 3030 m MD AHUROA SOUTH B-1 ST1

The Mangahewa Formation is comprised primarily of claystone, interbedded with minor layers of siltstone, sandstone and coal seams.

CLAYSTONE: The claystone varies in colour from brownish grey to brownish black and light olive grey to olive grey. The cuttings are firm to moderately hard and are sub-blocky to blocky in form. The claystone is non to moderately calcareous, becoming more calcareous towards the base of the section. The claystone grades to siltstone in parts.

SILTSTONE: The siltstone is light olive grey to brownish grey and brownish black. The cuttings are firm to moderately hard and sub-fissile to blocky in form. The siltstone is very carbonaceous in parts with coal laminae observed. There are trace amounts of very fine quartz grains in parts. The siltstone in part grades to claystone and sandstone.

SANDSTONE: The sandstone is light grey to yellow grey friable aggregates. The grain size ranges from very fine lower to fine lower. The grains are sub-angular to rounded, and are moderately sorted. Silty matrix is abundant in the sandstone. There is poor visible porosity.

text:
COAL SEAM: The coal is black in colour and brittle to firm. The cuttings are sub-fissile to blocky in structure and have a hackly fracture pattern. The coal has an earthy to vitreous lustre and is argillaceous in part.

The section of the Manganui Formation observed (the lower contact was not reached) is entirely claystone.

CLAYSTONE: The claystone is olive grey to olive black at the top of the section, then changes abruptly to medium grey to dark grey in colour, giving a clear indication of the change in the Manganui Formation. The claystone is blocky in structure with trace amounts of calcite veins noted in parts. The claystone is very slightly to slightly calcareous at the top of the section becoming non-calcareous with depth

Seals in the Taranaki Basin generally consist of marine mudstones, which form top seals and internal seals to hydrocarbon bearing reservoirs. In the Ahuroa/Piakau area, the reservoir sands are juxtaposed against Manganui mudstones along the main thrust to the west.

A paleontologist from GNS was on-site to evaluate samples obtained while drilling. The relatively short stratigraphic sections of Ahuroa South B-1 and Ahuroa South B-1 ST1 were examined, mainly to confirm that the well had penetrated the main thrust fault. Samples from the interval 3185 to 3245 m Ahuroa South B-1 were examined on-site. The remaining samples from Ahuroa South B-1 and all samples from Ahuroa South B-1 ST1 were examined at GNS.

Paleontology confirmed that both well bores penetrated the major thrust fault (Ahuroa Thrust). In the Ahuroa South B-1, 9 samples spanning the interval from 3185 - 3370 m TD, were examined. The section consists of upper Whaingaroan sediments of the Otaraoa and Tariki Formations, resting unconformably on un-dated, but probably upper Arnold Series, Kapuni Group sediments, which are, in turn, in fault contact with middle Altonian Manganui Formation (footwall).

Ahuroa South B-1 ST1 samples were taken from intervals 2970 - 3085 m (TD). The section consists of upper Whaingaroan sediments of the Otaraoa and Tariki Formations, resting unconformably on un-dated, but probably upper Arnold Series, Kapuni Group sediments, which are in turn, in fault contact with middle Altonian to possibly lower Southland Series Manganui Formation.

For the full report, see Appendix II.

Continuous 24-hour mud logging service was supplied by Baker Hughes Inteq. Mud logging commenced at surface casing (659 m) and continued to TD (3370 m/ 3085 m MD ST1). The following services were provided:

Spot samples were also taken at drill breaks / gas peaks, or on request from Geologist.

Distribution of cuttings samples was as follows:

Ministry of Economic Development: 1 set Washed and air-dried cuttings samples (Set E). Two (2) sets Unwashed and air-dried cuttings samples. (Sets A & B)

Swift Energy New Zealand Limited: 1 set Washed and oven-dried cuttings samples (Set D). One (1) set Unwashed and air-dried cuttings samples (Set C).

text:
Bottom hole temperatures were recorded during logging. Using the wireline logs, a bottom hole temperature of 88°C was recorded at 3218.4 m TVD (3374 m MD). Assuming an ambient surface temperature of 20°C, the geothermal gradient for the section penetrated is 21.13°C/km.

No check shots were run in Ahuroa South B-1 / ST1

Detailed petrophysical analysis was carried out over the target zones.

Drilled with OBM

OH Logged (Schlumberger)

Tariki Sand was encountered at 2714.0 m – 3002.0 m MD (Upper Tariki) and 3017.0 – 3131.0 m MD (Lower Tariki). A petrophysical analysis was not run on the Tariki sand given the results of the Piakau North A-1 well-bores. Wireline logs clearly showing wet Tariki sands with possible high residual hydrocarbon saturations, made difficult to quantify due to effects of OBM. It was noted however, that the Tariki sand had thickened substantially in this northerly direction relative to Piakau North.

Drilled with OBM

OH Logged (Schlumberger)

McKee Sand was encountered at 3231.0 – 3245.0 m MD. Unfortunately the McKee sand had thinned dramatically in this location and wire-line logs depicted a wet sand signature. A petrophysical analysis confirmed this, with zero netpay being interpreted.

The result from this well, added further weight to the local OWC existing at -2777 m TVDSS. As a result Ahuroa South B-1 was sidetracked in an updip location hoping to find a thickened McKee sand section and above the OWC.

Drilled with OBM

OH Logged (Schlumberger)

Tariki Sand was encountered at 2669.0 – 2929.0 m MD (Entire Tariki). A petrophysical analysis was not run on the Tariki sand given the results of the Piakau North A-1 well-bores and Ahuroa South B-1. A revised geological picture suggests that the McKee sand both thins to the north and to the west in the Ahuroa South area.

text:
Ahuroa South B-1 was spudded from 30m at 14:00 hrs on the 5th of October 2005 and was drilled to a total depth (TD) of 3370m with five drill bits. A Kelly system mounted on an Ingersol Rand Truck was used to drill this well. Unless otherwise stated, all depths in this report are measured in meters along hole below the Rotary Kelly Bushing (BRKB).

12.25" Hole Section: Prior to drilling the 12.25" hole section, independent contractors had set the 13.375" Conductor at 30m. One bit was used to drill the 12.25" section in one bit run.

NB-1 was run in and drilled from 30m to 659m. The 9.625" Casing was run in and cemented with the casing shoe set at 652m. Blow out preventers were installed and pressure tested. The mudlogging unit was rigged up and was online from 659m for the 8.5" Hole section.

NB3 a REED DSX104HG drilled out the cement, float and 3m of new formation. After conditioning the mud and performing a leak off test new hole was drilled with regular sliding required to build angle. NB3 drilled without incident to the 7" casing point at 2399m. Wiper trips were carried out at 1280m and 1826m. The bit was pulled out of hole and the following Schlumberger wireline logs run;

Run 1: PEX, HRLA, BHC; was run to a depth of 2398m

RR3 with a stripped down BHA was run into hole for hole cleaning prior to running the 7" casing. Once on bottom it was decided to drill another 4m. Then the BHA was pulled in preparation for running the 7" casing.

NB4 a Reed DSX516M-B1PDC bit was run in and drilled 6" hole from 2403m. After drilling out the 7" shoe and 3m of new hole, the mud was circulated and conditioned before an FIT test performed to an EMW of 10.5ppg at 2395m. New hole was then drilled, sliding and rotating as required. At 2787m a wiper trip was made back to the shoe. The hole was found to be in good condition when running back in. Rotary drilling continued with several slides and at regular intervals LCM sweeps pumped. NB4 drilled to 2903m where it was pulled due to poor penetration rates and problems sliding.

NB5 a Reed DSX516M-B1 PDC bit was run in along with a new mud motor and MWD probe. However due to MWD failure, the assembly was pulled out of hole and was re-run with a replacement MWD probe. Drilling alternated between sliding and rotating until 3006m after which there was no sliding as the reservoir section was approaching. A 17 stand wiper trip was made at 3182m. At 3296m a 1m coal stringer caused tight hole, the assembly was pulled to remove the motor and MWD tool due to the risk of further problems with possible coal lithologies.

NB6 a Reed DSX413M-A2 PDC bit was run in at 3296m and drilled to 3370m TD. The well was circulated clean and a four stand wiper trip performed before NB6 was pulled out of the hole.

A single wireline logging suite was then run:

Run 1: PEX-AIT-BHC was run to TD

After the wire line logging was completed a mule shoe and 2-7/8" tubing assembly was run-in on 3.5" drill pipe. Upon reaching the shoe, the Kelly was attached and the hole was slowly circulated, running in then continued to 2526m. The borehole was conditioned at this depth, by circulating the mud while reciprocating the pipe. Halliburton Cementing Unit was then lined up to the hole and a cement plug was set as per instructions. The mule shoe was pulled up to 2242m and the mud circulated, there were no cement returns. The Cement stinger was pulled out of hole and the excess 3-1/2" drillpipe laid out. Pulling out of hole continued, racking back the remaining drillpipe in the derrick. An assembly was run to drill out the cement and polish the plug before kicking off Ahuroa South B-1 ST-1.

SBM 8.5 – 8.7 ppg

Claystone, Siltstone, Sandstone

After the 7" casing had been run in and cemented and the BOPs tested, the mud system was changed to synthetic based mud. NB4 was made up and run in the hole picking up singles of 3.5" drill pipe. The MWD tool was shallow tested on entering the hole. The assembly was tripped in without incident tagging the float collar at 2395m. Cement, the shoe track, shoe and rat hole were drilled out to 2398m. The SBM mud was then circulated and conditioned prior to a leak off test (the water based mud was displaced to SBM during the cementing of the 7" casing). When the SBM had been weighted up to 8.5ppg, Howco were rigged up and performed a leak off test to an EMW of 11.5ppg. Drilling of the 6.0" section then proceeded, with 5bbl sweeps pumped at regular intervals. At 2787m bottoms up was circulated, the well was flow checked (static) then a slug pumped and a wiper trip was made back to the shoe. The hole was found to be in good condition when running back in. Bottoms up was circulated prior to drilling ahead. Rotary drilling continued with some short slides to maintain angle. 5 to 10bbl sweeps were pumped every third joint drilled. At 2903m the decision made to pull out of hole for a change of bit due to poor ROP and difficulty in sliding. A sweep was pumped and circulated out before pumping a slug and pulling

out of the hole. Once at the shoe at 2382m the well was flowchecked (static), and the assembly was tripped out of the hole. At surface the bit, motor and MWD were changed out and the Stabilizer was removed from the BHA before running in the hole with NB5.

204 joints of 7" casing were run in the hole open ended to reduce losses. Losses during the trip in amounted to 60bbl. A Circ Swedge was made up on the last joint, however tight hole was encountered at 2397m. While circulating, the pipe was worked in an attempt to work it free without success. The Circ Swedge was removed with difficulty and the cement head rigged up. Howco were lined up and the surface lines were pressure tested to 4000psi. After pumping a 38bbl water spacer the bottom plug was dropped, this was followed by 26bbl of water. 88bbl of 11.8ppg Lead cement slurry was pumped, followed by 178bbl of 15.6ppg tail. After dropping the top plug the cement was displaced with 20bbl of water and 280bbl synthetic mud. The plugs were bumped with 2200psi maintained for 10 minutes.

text:
Formation Evaluation of Ahuroa South B-1 commenced after the 9.625" casing shoe. Samples were collected in the 8.5" section (659m to 2403m) and also in the 6" section (2403m to 3370m). A Geological Society of America colour chart with Munsell colour chips was used for descriptions. The samples are described in the Mud Log using the standard abbreviations of Baker Hughes Inteq (N.Z. Ltd)

Flame Ionisation Total Gas and Chromatograph Detectors were used for gas analyses. During the course of the well, all gas equipment was calibrated regularly and spot samples were taken as required for more precise lithological evaluation.

The lithologies intersected in Ahuroa South B-1 are summarized below. All depths are in mAHT unless otherwise stated. For more detailed descriptions, see Appendix 1, Formation Evaluation Log.

The formation tops were picked on the basis of drilling data and samples.

Ahuroa South B-1 was drilled with KCl water based mud from 653m to 2403m then with 80% SBM from 2403m to 3370m TD.

The Urenui Formation was predominantly Claystone with Siltstone, Sandstone and Limestone beds.

CLAYSTONE: The Claystone was greenish grey to dark greenish grey, light bluish grey, medium grey and olive grey. The cuttings were predominantly very soft to soft, although they ranged from very soft to firm. They were largely amorphous to blocky. The Claystone was generally non calcareous but was slightly to very calcareous in parts. Accessories included a trace to minor presence of shell fragments in parts, trace to common very fine lower to fine upper quartz sand grains in parts, and minor to common glauconite pellets. This Claystone had an arenaceous nature in parts.

SILTSTONE: The Siltstone was olive grey in colour. The cuttings were soft and were amorphous to sub-blocky. The Siltstone was non calcareous and graded to Sandstone.

SANDSTONE: The Sandstone was mainly unconsolidated, transparent to translucent, quartz grains, with aggregates that were predominantly coloured light olive grey to greenish grey and medium bluish grey in parts. The aggregates were mostly firm to hard, although they ranged from soft to hard. The grain size ranged from very fine lower to medium lower, predominantly very fine upper to fine upper. They were sub-angular to sub-rounded in shape, and were moderately to well sorted. The Sandstone had an argillaceous cement in some parts and calcite cement in others, and was moderately to very calcareous in parts. Accessories included minor to common levels of glauconite, traces of shell fragments, and traces of mica. The Sandstone had poor inferred porosity.

LIMESTONE: The Limestone was predominantly white to light grey. The cuttings were firm to hard and sub-blocky in shape. The Limestone was arenaceous and the grains were very fine upper to fine lower in size. There was a minor component of shell fragments. The Limestone graded to Sandstone.

Total gas ranged from: 0.00%-0.28%.

No significant Gas Peaks were observed.

The Mt Messenger Formation was predominantly Claystone inter-bedded with Sandstone, Siltstone and Limestone.

CLAYSTONE: The Claystone was predominantly light olive grey to olive grey, though it was greenish grey to dark greenish grey, medium bluish grey, and medium dark grey in parts. It was very soft to firm, and the cuttings were sub-blocky to blocky in form. There was an arenaceous component to the Claystone, with traces of quartz sand grains ranging in size from very fine lower to very fine upper. The Claystone was slightly to very calcareous in parts and graded to Siltstone.

text:
The Tikorangi Formation was primarily Limestone with Siltstone interbeds.

LIMESTONE: The Limestone ranged in colour from white to light grey and olive grey. The Limestone was arenaceous in nature. The cuttings were generally very soft to firm, but were hard in parts and were sub-blocky to blocky in form. Traces of pyrite were present at the top of the formation. The Limestone graded to Siltstone, and also graded to Claystone at the top of the section.

SILTSTONE: The Siltstone ranged in colour from medium grey, medium bluish grey, olive grey, and greenish grey to dark greenish grey. The cuttings were soft to hard and were sub-blocky to blocky in form. The Siltstone was moderately to very calcareous. There were minor amounts of carbonaceous material in parts. It graded to Claystone and Limestone in parts.

Total gas ranged from: 0.05%-0.10%.

No significant gas peaks were observed.

For the purpose of this of this log the Otaraoa Formation has been split into three parts; thus enabling a distinct description of the Tariki Sandstone Member. These parts are: Upper Otaraoa, Tariki Member, and Lower Otaraoa.

The Upper Otaraoa Formation consists of Siltstone at the top of the section becoming mainly Claystone towards the base of the section, with Limestone inter-beds.

CLAYSTONE: The Claystone was light olive grey to olive black, dark greenish grey and medium grey. The cuttings ranged from soft to hard, though predominantly soft to firm. They were sub-blocky to blocky in shape. There was a trace to common component of calcite veins, and the Claystone was slightly to very calcareous, though predominantly moderately calcareous. The Claystone graded to Siltstone in parts.

SILTSTONE: The colour of the Siltstone was predominantly light olive grey to olive grey, although it was greenish grey to dark greenish grey and bluish grey in parts. The cuttings were soft to firm although they were hard in parts. They were sub-blocky to blocky in form. The Siltstone was argillaceous in parts, and also had a minor component of carbonaceous material in parts. The Siltstone was moderately to very calcareous throughout the section, however it gradually became less calcareous towards the base of the section. The Siltstone graded to Claystone and Limestone in parts.

LIMESTONE: The Limestone was olive grey to medium grey in colour. The cuttings were very soft to hard and were sub-blocky to blocky in form. The Limestone was arenaceous and graded to Siltstone.

The Tariki Formation was Sandstone with Siltstone, Claystone and Limestone beds.

SANDSTONE: The Sandstone was predominantly transparent to translucent quartz, with some white to dark grey, and yellowish grey aggregates. It was mostly unconsolidated, with a minor amount of soft to very hard aggregates. The grains ranged in size from very fine lower to coarse upper, and were sub-angular to rounded in shape. The grains were predominantly moderately to well sorted, although there were some poorly sorted examples. The cement was calcareous and there were trace amounts of glauconite, coal and carbonaceous material present in parts. Rock flour was also common in the cuttings. The Sandstone had poor to good inferred porosity.

SILTSTONE: The Siltstone was olive grey to olive black, and light to dark grey in parts. The cuttings were firm and sub-blocky to blocky in shape. The Siltstone had a slightly to moderately calcareous character and graded to Claystone in parts.

CLAYSTONE: The Claystone was light olive grey to olive grey, and was dark grey in parts. The cuttings ranged from very soft to hard although were mainly soft to firm. Cuttings were predominantly sub-blocky to blocky in form, although amorphous in parts. The Claystone ranged from non calcareous to moderately calcareous and graded to Siltstone in parts.

LIMESTONE: The Limestone was white to light grey. The cuttings ranged from soft to firm and were sub-blocky to blocky. The Limestone was arenaceous in parts, and had minor to common amounts of very fine upper to medium upper quartz grains. The Limestone graded to very calcareous Sandstone.

Total gas ranged from: 0.10% - 0.85%. Background gas: 0.21%-0.40%.

The Lower Otaraoa consisted of interbedded Claystone and Siltstone with minor amounts of Sandstone.

CLAYSTONE: The Claystone was light olive grey to olive grey in colour. The cuttings were soft to firm, with occasional very hard cuttings in parts. Their form was sub-blocky to blocky. The Claystone was slightly to moderately calcareous, and graded to Limestone at the top of the section. The Claystone also graded to Siltstone in parts.

SILTSTONE: The Siltstone was coloured dark greenish grey to greenish black. The cuttings ranged from soft to firm and were sub-blocky to blocky in form. Glauconite was common in the Siltstone. It was very calcareous, and graded to Claystone.

SANDSTONE: The Sandstone was loose transparent to translucent Quartz. The grains ranged in size from very fine lower to fine upper, were sub rounded and were moderately sorted. There was fair inferred porosity in the Sandstone.

The McKee Formation consisted of interbedded Sandstone and Siltstone.

SANDSTONE: The Sandstone was light grey to yellow grey friable aggregates. The grains ranged in size from very fine lower to fine lower. The grains were sub-angular to sub-rounded in shape and moderately well sorted. There was abundant silty matrix present, and traces of loose transparent to translucent quartz. There was poor visible porosity observed.

SILTSTONE: The Siltstone was mostly white to yellowish grey, but was also dark greenish grey to greenish black. The cuttings were sub-blocky to blocky in shape and soft to firm. Glauconite was common with the lighter Siltstone. The darker Siltstone was very calcareous, and the lighter was slightly calcareous in parts. The Siltstone graded to Sandstone.

Total gas ranged from: 0.24%-0.27%.

No significant Gas peaks were observed.

The Mangahewa formation is comprised primarily of Claystone, interbedded with minor layers of Siltstone. Sandstone and Coal seams. The lower contact of this formation is marked by the Ahuroa Thrust system.

CLAYSTONE: The Claystone varied in colour from brownish grey to brownish black and light olive grey to olive grey. The cuttings were firm to moderately hard and were sub-blocky to blocky in form. The Claystone was non-calcareous to moderately calcareous, becoming more calcareous towards the base of the section. The Claystone graded to Siltstone in parts.

SILTSTONE: The Siltstone was light olive grey to brownish grey and brownish black. The cuttings were firm to moderately hard and sub-fissile to blocky in shape. The Siltstone was very carbonaceous in parts and had coal laminae. There were also traces of very fine quartz grains in parts. The siltstone graded to Claystone.

SANDSTONE: The Sandstone was light grey to yellow grey aggregates. The aggregates were friable. The grain size ranged from very fine lower to fine lower. The grains were sub-angular to rounded and moderately sorted. Silty matrix was abundant in the Sandstone. The Sandstone had poor visible porosity.

COAL SEAM: The coal was black in colour and brittle to firm. The cuttings were sub-fissile to blocky in structure and had a hackly fracture pattern. The Coal had an earthy to vitreous lustre and was argillaceous in part.

text:
After setting a cement plug in Ahuroa South B-1 from 2526 to 2356m and dressing the cement to 2400m, Ahuroa South B-1 ST-1 was kicked off at 18:00hrs on the 11th of November 2005 and drilled to a total depth of 3085m in three bit runs. 8.5ppg – 8.7ppg synthetic based mud system was used to drill Ahuroa South B-1 ST-1. All depths in this report are in meters unless otherwise specified, measured along hole below the Rotary Kelly Bushing (BRKB).

6" Hole Section: This section was drilled with four bits in four bit runs.

NB8 a new Smith XR+ rock bit was run in to dress the top of the cement plug and kicked off the sidetrack at 2400m, using synthetic based mud initially weighed at 8.5ppg. At 2433m depth however, the bit was pulled due to poor penetration rates and inaccurate MWD surveys (it was determined that the directional probe high side correction had been entered incorrectly).

NB9, a Reed PDC bit was made up on the same steerable assembly as previous. Drilling the 6" sidetrack hole continued rotating and sliding, steering the bit through the desired wellpath. Hi-Vis sweeps were pumped and circulated at regular intervals for borehole cleaning. A six stand wiper trip was conducted at 2742m, with no overpull or drag recorded, indicating the hole to be in good condition. The mud weight was increased to 8.7ppg as the background gas and volume of liberated gases increased. NB9 was pulled at 2874m in order to change the bit.

NB10, a 6" Smith GeoDiamond bit was picked up along with a new mudmotor and MWD tool. The bit was run in to 2414m where the bit took weight. The Kelly was picked up and the minor tight spots encountered were worked through to 2430m. The trip in continued without incident. Drilling continued with regular 5bbl Hi-Vis sweeps pumped. At 2993m the drillstring became momentarily stuck prior to making a pipe connection. The pipe was able to be worked free (20klbs overpull recorded). After adding Barablok to the system, the bit was slowly pulled back to 2986m and then reamed back to 2993m. Drilling continued from 2993m with a short wiper trip carried out from 3031m to 2868m. Ahuroa South B-1 ST-1 reached TD at 3085m. After conducting a wiper trip and ensuring that the hole was clean, the bit was pulled to surface.

Schlumberger were rigged up and the following Wireline logs run;

Preparations were then made to plug and abandon the well. A mule shoe and 15 joints of 2 7/8" tubing were picked up and run in hole to 2430m. A balance cement plug was then set from 2445m to 2345m. Vause Wireline Services was rigged up and CBL log was conducted from 1500m to 500m. 3 1/2" drillpipe were then run in to tag the top of the cement without success.

A second cement job with ESZV packer assembly was planned. 21 joints of 2 7/8" tubing were picked up and made up with ESZV packer assembly. The packer was run in the hole and set at 2365m. HowCo were rigged up and pumped 12bbbls of 15.8ppg Class G cement slurry. After displacing the cement with SBM, the ESZV was engaged (sting) and 6bbbls of cement pumped below it. The 2 7/8" tubing was then pulled back to 2235m. The SBM in the hole was then displaced to brine.

The wear bushing was retrieved and a test plug installed in the tubing spool. Rig down of BOP followed. After removing the BOP, the test plug was pulled out and the appropriate adapter flange and master valve installed. The casing and wellhead was pressure tested to 3000psi. Preparations were then made to move the rig.

NB9 was made up on the same assembly as previous and run in hole to just above the kick-off depth. The well was monitored on the trip tank (static) while the drilling line was slipped and cut. The bit was then run to bottom and drilling resumed, sliding and rotating as required. The mud weight was increased from 8.5ppg to 8.7ppg due to the slight increase in background gas. 5bbl Hi-Vis sweeps were pumped at regular intervals to aid hole cleaning. At 2742m a six stand wiper trip was carried out, the borehole was found to be in good condition with no overpull or drag encountered. The bit was run back to bottom and drilling continued with reducing penetration rates. At 2874m, NB9 was pulled out after drilling 441m in 100.2 on-bottom drilling hours. The subsequent trip indicated good borehole condition, with no overpull encountered and correct pipe displacement recorded for the trip out.

NB10 was made up on a new BHA with a new mudmotor and MWD tool. The bit was run in until above kick-off point where the drilling line was slipped and cut. The trip in continued with the bit encountering a tight spot from 2414m to 2430m which had to be worked through. The bit was run in without incident and the last single washed down to bottom. Drilling proceeded from 2874m to 2993m where the drillstring became stuck momentarily prior to making a connection (coal interbeds earlier encountered around 2985m were the likely cause). text:
The lithologies intersected in the sidetrack borehole Ahuroa South B-1 ST-1 are summarized below. For more detailed descriptions, see Appendix 1, Formation Evaluation Log.

The formation tops were picked on the basis of drilling data and samples.

Ahuroa South B-1 ST-1 was drilled with 8.5ppg to 8.7ppg synthetic based mud (SBM) from kick-off at 2400m to final depth at 3085m.

OTARAOA FORMATION: 2010m-2983m (1939m-2878m TVD)

For the purpose of this of this log the Otaraoa Formation has been split into two parts, enabling a distinct description of the Tariki Sandstone Member. These parts are; Upper Otaraoa, and the Tariki Member.

UPPER OTARAOA: 2010m-2665m (1939m-2598m TVD)

The Upper Otaraoa Formation consists of Siltstone at the top of the section becoming mainly Claystone towards the base of the section.

CLAYSTONE: The Claystone was light olive grey to olive black, brownish grey and medium grey were also commonly observed. The cuttings ranged from soft to hard, though predominantly soft to firm and were sub-blocky to blocky in shape. There was a trace to common component of calcite veins and the Claystone was slightly to very calcareous, though predominantly moderately calcareous. The Claystone graded to Siltstone in parts.

SILTSTONE: The colour of the Siltstone was predominantly light olive grey to olive grey, although it was greenish grey to dark greenish grey and bluish grey in parts. The cuttings were soft to firm though they were hard in parts and were sub-blocky to blocky in form. The Siltstone was argillaceous in parts and also had a minor component of carbonaceous material in parts. The Siltstone was moderately to very calcareous throughout the section, however it gradually became less calcareous towards the base of the section. On occasion the Siltstone graded to the above Claystone.

Total gas ranged from: 0.09%-0.34%.

No significant gas peaks were observed.

TARIKI MEMBER: 2665m-2983m (2563m-2878m TVD)

The Tariki Formation was Sandstone with Siltstone and Claystone inter beds.

SANDSTONE: The Sandstone was predominantly transparent to translucent quartz, with some white to dark grey, and yellowish grey aggregates. It was mostly unconsolidated, with a minor amount of soft to very hard aggregates. The grains ranged in size from very fine lower to coarse upper, and were sub-angular to rounded. The grains were predominantly moderately to well sorted, although there were some poorly sorted examples. The cement was calcareous and there were trace amounts of glauconite, coal and carbonaceous material present in parts. There was poor to good inferred porosity.

text:
SILTSTONE: The Siltstone was olive grey to olive black, and light to dark grey in parts. The cuttings were firm and were sub-blocky to blocky in shape. The Siltstone was slightly to moderately calcareous and graded to Claystone in parts.

CLAYSTONE: The Claystone was light olive grey to olive grey and dark grey in parts. Cuttings ranged from very soft to hard although were mainly soft to firm. The cuttings were predominantly sub-blocky to blocky in form, although were amorphous in parts. The Claystone ranged from non to moderately calcareous and graded to Siltstone in parts.

Total gas ranged from: 0.09% - 0.80%. Background gas: 0.12%-0.65%.

The Mangahewa formation was comprised primarily of Claystone, interbedded with minor layers of Siltstone Sandstone and Coal seams. The lower contact of this formation is marked by the Ahuroa Thrust system.

CLAYSTONE: The Claystone varied in colour from brownish grey to brownish black and light olive grey to olive grey. The cuttings were firm to moderately hard and were sub-blocky to blocky in form. The Claystone was non to moderately calcareous, becoming more calcareous towards the base of the section. The Claystone graded to Siltstone in parts.

text:
SILTSTONE: The Siltstone was light olive grey to brownish grey and brownish black. The cuttings were firm to moderately hard and sub-fissile to blocky in form. The Siltstone was very carbonaceous in parts with coal laminae observed. There were trace amounts of very fine quartz grains in parts. The Siltstone in part graded to Claystone and Sandstone.

SANDSTONE: The Sandstone was light grey to yellow grey friable aggregates. The grain size ranged from very fine lower to fine lower. The grains were sub-angular to rounded, and were moderately sorted. Silty matrix was abundant in the Sandstone. There was poor visible porosity.

COAL SEAM: The coal was black in colour and brittle to firm. The cuttings were sub-fissile to blocky in structure and had a hackly fracture pattern. The Coal had an earthy to vitreous lustre and was argillaceous in part.

Total gas ranged from: 0.27%-0.54%. Background gas: 0.13%-0.58%.

The section of the Manganui Formation observed (the lower contact was not reached) was entirely Claystone.

CLAYSTONE: The Claystone was olive grey to olive black at the top of the section, then changed abruptly to medium grey to dark grey in colour, giving a clear indication of the change in the Manganui formation. The Claystone was blocky in structure with trace amounts of calcite veins noted in parts. The Claystone was very slightly to slightly calcareous at the top of the section becoming non calcareous with depth

Total gas ranged from: 0.22%-0.78%.

No significant Gas Peaks were observed.

Drill 12 1/4" hole to 650m and set 9 5/8" casing.

Drill out with 8 1/2" directional assembly then build at 3°/30m to 19.6 degrees on 136 degrees azimuth by 850m, then hold to 7" casing point @ 2600m ( later changed to 2400m ) .

Drill out 7" casing with 6" directional assembly and hold to TD @ 3600m, intersecting Target at 3027mTVD.

12 1/4" Section:

Due to the proximity of another producing well, it was considered necessary to run a steerable assembly in the 12 1/4" section. The well was spudded at with a conventional rotary assembly, with W/L surveys taken every 50m to track deviation, and this was used to 200m where it was pulled and replaced with a steerable assembly. No problems were encountered on this section and the well was drilled to 659m with minimal slide/corrections to keep it on line.

8 1/2" Section:

The build and turn was achieved as per the plan with an average dogleg of 2.6°/30m. Inclination and azimuth was then held in the tangent section through to the 7" casing point at 2395m MD. Due to the nature of the formations in this area it was difficult to ascertain the rotary Bld / walk trend but toward the last 200m it appeared to have a slight Drop and Right walk although this could have been attributed to the considerable wear to the shoulder/gauge row of cutters on the bit.

6" Section:

BHA #4 performed well despite a strong 0.5°/30m drop and -1.0°/30m Right walk, in the rotary mode. The situation was made more difficult when the customer advised ( 300m from target ) that they only wanted to be in the top 1/2 of the target and they wanted to follow the line after the target through to TD. This assembly was pulled due to poor penetration rate at 2903m.

BHA #5 was run in but the MWD failed to respond when pumping commenced. At surface the impeller/stator was found to be plugged with LCM. From this depth on a screen was used in the drill string. This assembly at first had a rotary build rate of 0.3°/30m and a right walk of 0.7°/30m until 3050m MD, where the rotary tendency was to turn right at an average of between 1 - 3°/30m and drop between 0.5 - 1.0°/30m . It was necessary to wait for sections of faster ROP to slide in ( due to the aggressive nature of the bit ) & sliding results varied between 0.8 - 1.0°/30m after a 5-8m slide.

From 3100m onward no further corrections were attempted ( at operator's request ) as the well path was within projected boundaries.

Rotary drilling continued to 3297m where some tight hole was experienced on a connection, after drilling some stringers of coal, and it was decided to lay our directional tools out and proceed with a conventional rotary assembly.

Side track the well directly outside the 7" shoe (low side). Drop the inclination back past zero to 2.65 degrees in the opposite direction to intersect the new target.

BHA #1 2400 - 2433m MD

The well was sidetracked successfully during this interval. Time drilling began at 2400m MD and concluded at 2423m MD. Sliding continued from 2423 - 2429m MD and rotary mode was used through to 2433m MD. The survey from 2422.8m MD indicated a build in the well where all sliding and time drilling was to side track the well low side. Further investigation found the MWD tool offset data had not been updated from the previous probe run and subsequently was 147 degrees out. ROP with the Smith 117 was poor and the agreed bit hours were nearly up so the decision was made to POOH and rectify all shortcomings.

BHA #2 2433 -2874m MD

Sliding was easy and controllable during the drop and early part of the build, then as formations became harder sliding became very slow. In the Tariki ROP slowed to 1 - 3m/hr. During the low angle tangent section the assembly built angle at 1.05°/30m on average. There were two large azimuth swings toward the west at 2734m and 2849m MD. Despite 12 metres of sliding between 2830m and 2858m, the assembly still built only 1.05 degrees. The assembly was pulled due to motor hours. The hole was good during the trip out.

BHA # 3 2874m - 3085m

As expected with the new bit ROP doubled and slides although not easy with the interbedded formations were drilled at a faster ROP and only one 6m slide was needed to ensure a west side target penetration. Initial rotary drilling ROP varied between 2 - 10m/hr with 3-7k WOB through the Tariki, and Lower Otara claystone. The McKee sands did not develop and instead coals were hit at 2983m and stuck pipe stopped the drilling for 6 to 8hrs before working free and controlled drilling of 1-2m/hr continued for much of the remainder of the hole. The formations came in about 130m high and by the time the proposed target was hit at 3046.9m MD the Ahuroa thrust/fault had already been intersected at 3034m in the Manganui and rat hole to 3085m was drilled before the assembly was tripped out and laid out.

BHA #1 2400 - 2433m MD

The well was sidetracked successfully during this interval. Time drilling began at 2400m MD and concluded at 2423m MD. Sliding continued from 2423 - 2429m MD and rotary mode was used through to 2433m MD. The survey from 2422.8m MD indicated a build in the well where all sliding and time drilling was to side track the well low side. Further investigation found the MWD tool offset data had not been updated from the previous probe run and subsequently was 147 degrees out. ROP with the Smith 117 was poor and the agreed bit hours were nearly up so the decision was made to POOH and rectify all shortcomings.

BHA #2 2433 -2874m MD

Sliding was easy and controllable during the drop and early part of the build, then as formations became harder sliding became very slow. In the Tariki ROP slowed to 1 - 3m/hr. During the low angle tangent section the assembly built angle at 1.05°/30m on average. There were two large azimuth swings toward the west at 2734m and 2849m MD. Despite 12 metres of sliding between 2830m and 2858m, the assembly still built only 1.05 degrees. The assembly was pulled due to motor hours. The hole was good during the trip out.

BHA # 3 2874m - 3085m

As expected with the new bit ROP doubled and slides although not easy with the interbedded formations were drilled at a faster ROP and only one 6m slide was needed to ensure a west side target penetration. Initial rotary drilling ROP varied between 2 - 10m/hr with 3-7k WOB through the Tariki, and Lower Otara claystone. The McKee sands did not develop and instead coals were hit at 2983m and stuck pipe stopped the drilling for 6 to 8hrs before working free and controlled drilling of 1-2m/hr continued for much of the remainder of the hole. The formations came in about 130m high and by the time the proposed target was hit at 3046.9m MD the Ahuroa thrust/fault had already been intersected at 3034m in the Manganui and rat hole to 3085m was drilled before the assembly was tripped out and laid out.

text:
To drop angle and hit target in the North west quarter.

As expected with the new bit ROP doubled and slides although not easy with the interbedded formations were drilled at a faster ROP and only one 6m slide was needed to ensure a west side target penetration. Initial rotary drilling ROP varied between 2-10m/hr with 3-7k WOB through the Tariki and Lower Ahuroa claystone. The McKee sands didn't develop and instead coals were hit at 2983m and stuck pipe stopped the drilling for 6 to 8hrs before working free and controlled drilling continued for much of the remainder of the hole. The formations came in about 130m high and by the time the proposed target was hit at 3046m the Ahuroa thrust/fault had already been intersected at 3034m in the Manganui, and rat hole to 3085m was drilled before the assembly was tripped out and laid out.

No recommendations, the assembly worked well and achieved the desired result
